intro: Hello, explorer! I'm {name}, your mission guide. Today we're going to land on the Moon, at its south pole.
Why the Moon? It's the closest world to Earth, and a great place to learn how to live and work far from home.
Why the south pole? Some deep craters there never see the Sun, and they hide ice. Ice can become water to drink, air to breathe and fuel for rockets.
You can see the south pole in 3D or in 2D. Switch 3D to 2D at the top right of the Moon view to see it flat.
Two golden rules keep a lander alive. It needs sunlight for power, and it must see Earth to talk to us.
Rule 1: sunlight. At the south pole the Sun stays low, near the horizon, so hills and crater walls can block it. Our landing site must be a place the Sun's rays can reach.
Rule 2: Earth. Our lander talks to us by radio, and radio needs a clear path to Earth. From the south pole, Earth also sits low in the sky, so our site must be able to see it over the hills.
Both rules depend on when we land. The Sun and Earth move across the sky, so the time you choose decides which sites pass. Drag the time bar at the top to see how they change.
This graph shows the next 30 days for this site. Yellow means Sunlight, green means Earth in view, and cyan means both at once. A good landing time is cyan.
Click on the graph to move its bar and read the exact time. You can compare the different lunar sites at the same time here.

This box counts down to the next sunrise or sunset, and to the next Earthrise or Earthset. Stays in view means it does not change during the stay. Sunlight charges the lander, and Earth in view lets it talk to us, so these countdowns show when it has power and contact.
So many probes have landed on the Moon before, and some carried people too!
Switch on Historic sites to see where people landed before.
Click here to see all the missions that went to the Moon before.
You can explore the different sites. Tap any flag to read its story.
Look at IM-2 Athena. It missed its target by only about 250 meters.
It came down inside a cold, dark crater, lying on its side. With no sunlight on its panels, it could not recharge.

site.pick: It's time for your first mission! We want to land on the Moon on 16/11/2026. Pick a landing site in the list or click on it on the map.
site.good: Great choice! {site} has sunlight for the panels and Earth in view to talk to us. This lander will live.
site.noLink: {site} gets sunlight, but Earth is hidden behind the terrain. The lander would have power, but nobody could hear it. Try another site.
site.noSun: {site} can see Earth, but the Sun can't reach it. With no power, the lander would fall silent. Try another site.
site.neither: {site} is in shadow and can't see Earth. The lander would be dark and silent. Try another site.
site.darkWeek: Every spot is dark this week. Let's jump to a brighter one.

launch.cheer: Up we go! Hold on tight, the Moon is waiting.

anomaly.delay: Oh no, a storm on Earth held us back. We lifted off some days late.
anomaly.night: The Sun has already left {site}. The night ahead is longer than our battery.
anomaly.earth: From here, Earth hides behind the hills. Our messages cannot get home.
anomaly.contact: Silence. Earth has slipped behind the hills, and our words go unheard.

fix.intro: Every mission has a bump. Pick a lever and watch the verdict change.
fix.move: Higher ground sees the Sun sooner. Let's pack up and move.
fix.wait: Patience is a tool too. We will wait for the Sun to return.
fix.relay: A relay satellite will carry our words. It costs a lot, but it hears us.
fix.battery: A bigger battery for the dark. The lander grows heavier, though.
fix.noWait: No sunny day comes soon enough. Try another lever.
fix.go: Green at last! You turned a bad day into a good plan.
fix.notyet: Not yet. Try another lever, or combine two.

done.cheer: You did it, Space Planner. The Moon remembers brave choices.
